## Proof

Represent the torus as the product
$$T^2 = S^1 \times S^1.$$

A *cylinder* (ring-shaped region) is a space homeomorphic to $S^1 \times [0,1]$, i.e. an annulus. We embed such a cylinder in the torus as follows. Pick a proper closed arc $J \subset S^1$ (a closed interval embedded in the circle, not the whole circle), and set
$$C \;=\; S^1 \times J \;\subset\; S^1 \times S^1 \;=\; T^2.$$
Since $J \cong [0,1]$, we have $C \cong S^1 \times [0,1]$, a genuine cylinder. Geometrically $C$ is a tubular (collar) neighborhood of the essential (non-contractible) circle $S^1 \times \{\text{pt}\}$, a longitude of the torus.

We remove the **interior** of $C$ (so that a boundary remains), forming
$$M \;=\; T^2 \setminus \operatorname{int}(C).$$

Because $\operatorname{int}(C) = S^1 \times \operatorname{int}(J)$, the product structure gives
$$M \;=\; S^1 \times \bigl(S^1 \setminus \operatorname{int}(J)\bigr).$$

Now $J$ is a proper closed arc in $S^1$, so $\operatorname{int}(J)$ is a proper open arc, and its complement $S^1 \setminus \operatorname{int}(J)$ is a closed arc, homeomorphic to $[0,1]$. Hence
$$M \;\cong\; S^1 \times [0,1].$$

**Topological description of $M$.**

- $M \cong S^1 \times [0,1]$ is a **cylinder (annulus)**.
- It is **connected**, being the product of two connected spaces ($S^1$ and $[0,1]$).
- It is a **2-manifold with boundary**. Locally every interior point has a neighborhood homeomorphic to $\mathbb{R}^2$, and every boundary point has a neighborhood homeomorphic to a half-plane $\mathbb{H}^2$.
- Its **boundary** is
$$\partial M \;=\; S^1 \times \{0\} \;\sqcup\; S^1 \times \{1\},$$
the disjoint union of **two circles** (the two rim circles of the cylinder).

**Why the remainder is connected (non-separating removal).** The removed cylinder $C$ is a tubular neighborhood of the essential simple closed curve $\ell = S^1 \times \{\text{pt}\}$. An essential curve on a torus is non-separating: cutting the torus along $\ell$ produces a single annulus rather than two pieces. Removing a tubular neighborhood of $\ell$ has the same effect, so the complement $M$ is a single connected piece. (By contrast, removing a tubular neighborhood of a *contractible* curve would separate the torus into a disk and a punctured torus — two components — which is exactly the situation the problem excludes.)

**Conclusion.** Removing a cylinder (annulus) from the torus as a tubular neighborhood of an essential circle, taking out its interior, yields a space homeomorphic to $S^1 \times [0,1]$: a **cylinder (annulus)**, a connected 2-manifold whose boundary consists of two disjoint circles.
